newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Appeal result due in Korea's "trial of century".
newsitem.headline: Appeal result due in Korea's "trial of century".

text.p: South Korea's "trial of the century" hits another milestone on Monday when an appeals court passes judgement on a death sentence for former president Chun Doo Hwan and a 22-1/2 year jail term for his successor Roh Tae-woo.

Both are appealing convictions for mutiny, treason and bribery over a 1979 coup that launched Chun's political career, an army massacre in 1980 that crushed democratic opposition and massive corruption during their administrations.
The Hankook Ilbo newspaper on Sunday quoted one of Chun's lawyers as saying his state of mind was "transcendental" as he fought to escape the hangman's noose.
"If I open my eyes in the morning, it tells I am alive. If my eyes do not open, it tells I'm dead, doesn't it?" the lawyer quoted Chun as saying.
Verdicts are also expected in the cases of 14 former generals, 13 of whom were convicted for their roles in the bloody events dating from what Koreans now call the era of "military dictatorship".
One ex-general was acquitted in the first trial but prosecutors are seeking to overturn that verdict.

Judges are also due to rule on appeals by five business tycoons, including the chairman of Daewoo Group, found guilty of bribing Chun and Roh and six former presidential aides convicted for acting as bagmen for payments worth hundreds of millions of dollars to the Presidential Blue House.
State prosecutors argue Roh's jail term is too light, and want heavier punishment for the one-time military cronies.
Defendants can appeal higher to the Supreme Court, and hearings could drag until well into next year.

The most dramatic moment in the appeal came when a third former president, Choi Kyu-hah, an ailing recluse, hobbled into the court on a cane after being forced to turn up. But he mocked the proceedings by refusing to answer questions.
The marathon trial, part of President Kim Young-sam's campaign to "right the wrongs of history", has been overshadowed by fresh corruption scandals involving Kim's own cabinet.

Former Defence Minister Lee Yang-ho is on trial for accepting payments from a Daewoo Group unit after he was sacked in October. Last month, health minister Lee Sung-ho stepped down amid a corruption scandal involving his wife.

Few South Koreans believe Chun will hang, even if he exhausts the appeals process. An amnesty for both ex-presidents is seen likely before Kim's single term expires in 1998 after presidential elections next December.

As he prepares to anoint a chosen successor, Kim needs the support of rightwingers who once backed Chun and Roh and who are deeply unhappy at the social turmoil whipped up by Kim's drive to purge South Korea's corrupt legacy.

Hardliners have been strengthened by a political lurch to the right in South Korea. This was signalled in a public backlash against violent leftist campus protests and an anti-communist reaction to a North Korean submarine incursion in September.
The rallying ground for the right wing is the electorally critical southern city of Taegu and surrounding North Kyongsang province, Chun and Roh's former stronghold.
Judges will first deliver verdicts on the mutiny and treason convictions and then deal with the corruptions issues.

The businessmen are Kim Woo-choong, founding chairman of Daewoo Group, Choi Won-suk, head of Dong-Ah Group, Chang Jin-ho, chairman of Jinro Group, Chung Tae-soo, founding chairman of Hanbo Group and Daewoo Corp's Lee Kyung-hoon.
